title: Attribute test failures via baseline diff, not absolute counts
body: The full pytest suite has a large population (~140) of pre-existing failures in sandboxes lacking real backends (LanceDB/PostgreSQL) and where the embedding model can't load (SentenceTransformer/torch on Apple MPS: 'Cannot copy out of meta tensor' — set INQUIRY_EMBEDDING_DEVICE=cpu to dodge it). The suite also randomizes order (pytest-randomly), so failure positions and even which flaky tests fail shift run to run; absolute pass/fail counts are not comparable across runs. To decide whether a change introduced a regression, diff the FAILING-TEST SETS between your branch and origin/main with identical flags (e.g. via --junitxml + set difference), not the totals. Use -p no:randomly for a deterministic run.

title: uv.lock bumps churn markers when your uv is newer than origin/main's
body: Running `uv lock --upgrade-package X` with a uv newer than the one that generated the committed uv.lock regenerates the whole file, normalizing/simplifying redundant environment markers across packages unrelated to X (seen with cloud-sql-python-connector, scipy/numpy, hypothesis, nvidia-* CUDA, secretstorage). Why 'redundant': older uv emitted conservatively narrowed per-dependency markers (e.g. `python_full_version < '3.13'` on a sub-dep whose parent is already gated `< '3.13'`, or `>= '3.10.2'` floors implied by requires-python >=3.10); newer uv recomputes markers against the package's actual support range and drops the ones already implied by an enclosing marker or by requires-python. The installed set is identical (no package add/remove) and `uv lock --locked` still passes, so it's semantically benign — but it bloats a focused dependency PR's diff. For a minimal diff, regenerate with the same uv version that produced origin/main's lock; otherwise just note the benign churn in the PR/commit body so reviewers aren't surprised.

title: Connector registration is an import-time decorator side effect — fragile two ways
body: Connectors register via `@register_connector("name")` in their module; the registry's `_register_builtin_connectors()` only makes them reachable by *importing* the module (firing the decorator). Two consequences bit us in issue #82. (1) A connector whose module nothing imports is silently unregistered: `GCSConnector` carried `@register_connector("gcs")` but `_register_builtin_connectors()` never imported it (only s3/filesystem), so `get_connector("gcs")` raised KeyError despite the class existing — fix was to add the guarded `from ...gcs import GCSConnector` import. The lib check (gcsfs/s3fs) lives in `__init__`, not at module import, so registration works even without the cloud lib installed — only construction needs it. (2) Because Python caches modules, the decorator fires only on FIRST import; after `ConnectorRegistry.reset_instance()` the decorators do NOT re-fire, so `_register_builtin_connectors()` cannot restore s3/gcs (only the explicitly-registered filesystem/file). test_registry.py reset the singleton in autouse fixtures without restoring, leaking an empty registry to later test files — invisible while s3fs/gcsfs are absent (those registration tests skip) but a hard failure once the extras are installed. Robust test pattern: snapshot the registered factories at import time and re-register them on teardown; assert import-time registration in a fresh subprocess interpreter, not in-process (sibling tests that import the connector module pollute the in-process registry and make the assertion pass for the wrong reason).

title: fsspec connector URI scheme and fsspec protocol are independent
body: In an FsspecConnector subclass the `protocol=` passed to the base (what `fsspec.filesystem()` receives) and the URI scheme emitted by `_build_uri`/parsed by `_uri_to_path` are separate concerns. GCSConnector passes `protocol="gcs"` (gcsfs accepts it) but its `SourceItem.uri` scheme is cosmetic and feeds `SourceItem.protocol`. We aligned the URI scheme from `gs://` to `gcs://` to match the registered connector name, `item.protocol`, and the docs — without touching the fsspec protocol. Don't 'fix' one to match the other. Also note gcsfs's real `md5Hash` is base64-encoded (e.g. 'CY9rzUYh03PK3k6DJie09g=='), not hex; `base._extract_hash` passes it through verbatim (its `strip('"')` is S3-ETag cleanup), so mocks using plain ASCII hashes hide the real shape — pin the base64 pass-through explicitly.

title: Call-graph extraction must probe tree-sitter node fields/types per grammar, not hardcode Python's
body: The `queries/*.scm` files correctly capture calls for every language, but `_extract_call_info` and `_find_containing_definition[_key]` used to hardcode Python's grammar — the `function` field and `identifier`/`attribute` node types, and container types `function_definition`/`class_definition`/`method_definition`. So Java (`method_invocation` with `name`/`object` fields; containers `method_declaration`/`class_declaration`) and Rust (`field_expression` method calls; `function_item`/`impl_item`) produced ZERO `calls` edges even though entities extracted fine (issue #179). Fix: probe structure — prefer the `function` field (Python `call`, C-family/Go/Rust/TS/C# `call_expression`/`invocation_expression`), else fall back to `name`/`method` + `object`/`receiver` (Java, Ruby). Node type `call` is AMBIGUOUS: Python's has a `function` field, Ruby's has `method`/`receiver` — so a naive node-type dispatch silently regresses Ruby. Three more traps: (1) only add a node type to `_DEFINITION_NODE_TYPES` if it's captured as a processable `.def`/element — `arrow_function` (`@code_function.arrow`) and Rust `mod_item` (`@code_module`) are NOT, and would silently swallow the calls attributed to them; container byte-span must line up with an emitted `@code_*.def` element or the edge is dropped. (2) The collection loop de-dups DEFINITIONS via `seen_nodes` but did not de-dup CALLS — a call site captured under multiple query patterns (e.g. `cpp.scm` ships two byte-identical `@call.method` patterns; Java captures the same invocation as both `@call` and `@call.method`) double-counts. De-dup calls by call-node byte span. (3) When the `function` field holds a member/attribute accessor, its object/name subfields vary even for the SAME accessor node-type name: Rust `field_expression` uses `value` but C++'s uses `argument` (both `field` for the name); Go method calls use `selector_expression` (`operand`/`field`). Let the object slot list multiple candidate field names and take the first that resolves, else receiver metadata silently drops to empty — the target stays correct, so a target-only test won't catch it; assert `metadata['object']`. Regression tests live in tests/parsers/test_calls_extraction_multilang.py; the Python tests in test_relationship_extraction.py are the passing baseline.

title: Narrowing requires-python needs a full sweep of version statements
body: When you change the package's supported Python range (requires-python in pyproject.toml), the declared version lives in more than pyproject + README. Grep docs for package-level prerequisites ('Python X or higher', 'X+', 'Should be X+') and update every one — a missed line (e.g. docs/mcp/deployment.md System Requirements) keeps advertising a version you no longer support. Crucially, distinguish three classes before editing: (1) package-level supported-version statements — UPDATE these; (2) dependency-specific notes (e.g. 'cloud-sql-python-connector doesn't support 3.13' in docs/backends, docs/storage) — LEAVE, they track a library's own matrix; (3) language-feature notes ('deprecated in Python 3.10+' in docs/development/async-best-practices.md) — LEAVE, they track language behavior. Also verify the co-located declarations that may not exist: pyproject classifiers, [tool.ruff] target-version (inferred from requires-python when unset), [tool.mypy] python_version (a floor, unaffected by an upper bound), and any CI matrix. See K-0002 for the companion uv.lock regeneration gotcha.

title: Registry defaults built at import leak Config.load and mkdir into every process
body: A package __init__ that constructs its default registry entry at import (agentic_inquiry.watching did, via FileWatcher(file_tracker=FileTracker())) runs Config.load() and FileTracker's mkdir in every process that imports it, so pytest collection alone created ./.agentic-inquiry in cwd. Build the default in an _ensure_default_registered() called only by the lookups that need it (get_watcher('default'), get_watcher() with no default set, available_watchers()). Register it without set_default so a caller's default keeps precedence, and hold a threading.Lock around check-and-register because the import lock no longer serializes it. Test in a fresh interpreter through test_import_hygiene._run (scratch cwd and HOME); swap the module's FileWatcher global for a counting stub, since a real build costs about 3.5s. Precedence tests must call the building path while a caller default is set, or a set_default=True mutant still passes. agentic_inquiry/cache/__init__.py registers its lazy default with set_default=True and builds it on every get_cache(), named lookups included.
